\title{C-TreePO: Compression Tree Preference Optimization}
\author{Mitchell Linegar}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Preference optimization on long documents is hard because hierarchical summarization can destroy the task signal before the optimizer ever sees the document.
We introduce \emph{Compression Tree Preference Optimization} (C-TreePO), which treats recursive summarization as a learned mergeable sketch: split a document into contiguous blocks, summarize locally, and audit whether each merge preserves the task oracle.
The framework is organized around three local laws: each leaf summary must preserve the evidence the task depends on, re-summarizing a stored summary must not change that evidence, and split-then-merge must preserve the same cross-span interactions as summarize-together.
Our main results form a ladder: local validity yields root-level oracle preservation and schedule invariance, adding downstream factorization yields the same population target as full-document DPO/GRPO training, and adding calibration and sampling assumptions turns sampled audits into an empirical preference-gap certificate. The training and audit paths read as two sides of one formal equivalence: supervising with local-law weights projects the learned summarizer onto the subspace where the laws hold, and auditing with node samples is the finite-sample estimator of the structural assumption that the approximation error is zero exactly on that subspace.
We demonstrate the mechanism on a Markov changepoint color-transition counting task, where decomposing the document into a tree of smaller subproblems matches or improves on a flat Fourier Neural Operator baseline across the full range of supervision budgets, including when only $10\%$ of documents receive root-level labels.
The sufficient statistic for this task is simple---a triple of integers at each node---but the same structural mechanism extends to settings where the local summaries are high-dimensional learned representations.
We instantiate that extension on political-text measurement at two levels of supervision. A prompt-only C-Tree over a single open-weight model matches a three-frontier-LLM ensemble on the Manifesto Project benchmark of expert-survey party positions (macro Pearson $0.829$ vs.\ $0.817$) at two orders of magnitude lower compute. And because the Manifesto corpus carries expert category codes on every quasi-sentence, the same trees admit gold oracle values at every node: trained on that supervision, a small neural-operator summarizer composes lawfully on every signal-dense policy dimension, and seeding it with sampled leaf states recovers the full document rollup at Pearson $0.95$.
\end{abstract}
